definitions.definition: The canonical scripture: the words of the Tīrthaṅkara as composed by the gaṇadharas and elders, fixed at Valabhī — forty-five texts for Mūrtipūjakas, thirty-two for Sthānakavāsīs and Terāpanthīs.

The Digambaras hold the original āgama (the Aṅgas and Pūrvas) lost; the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and Kaṣāyapāhuḍa preserve parts of it and are called 'āgama', and the works of later ācāryas in the four anuyogas serve as scripture.
One of the twelve 'limbs' of the canon (dvādaśāṅga, the 'basket of the gaṇin') composed by the gaṇadharas; eleven survive for the Śvetāmbaras, the twelfth (Dṛṣṭivāda) is lost.

cross_language.note: the twelve limbs as a whole

notes: Disambiguated from other senses of 'aṅga' (limb of yoga; Vīraśaiva devotee).

definitions.definition: A 'subsidiary limb': one of twelve aṅga-external canonical texts, each paired with an Aṅga (Aupapātika with the Ācārāṅga, and so on).

A canonical text of monastic law, fixing the atonements for transgressions; named from 'cheda' (cutting of seniority), one of the atonements. Six for Mūrtipūjakas, four for Sthānakavāsīs; traditionally studied only by mature monks.
A 'root' text studied first by new monks — the Uttarādhyayana, Daśavaikālika, Āvaśyaka and Piṇḍa- or Ogha-niryukti (Mūrtipūjaka list); the Sthānakavāsīs count the Nandī and Anuyogadvāra here instead.

A 'miscellaneous' canonical text, ten in the standard Mūrtipūjaka list (Catuḥśaraṇa, Āturapratyākhyāna and others), many on devotion and the discipline of dying; the Nandī says there were as many prakīrṇakas as disciples of a Tīrthaṅkara. Rejected by Sthānakavāsīs and Terāpanthīs.
An 'appendix' text of the canon: the Nandī and the Anuyogadvāra, which introduce knowledge and the method of exposition.
One of the fourteen 'former' texts, said to have been taught before the Aṅgas and contained in the Dṛṣṭivāda; known in full last by the śrutakevalin Bhadrabāhu and then gradually lost.
Portions of the second and fifth Pūrvas survive as the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and Kaṣāyapāhuḍa.
One who knows the whole scripture (all the Aṅgas and fourteen Pūrvas) and so is 'omniscient in scripture' though not by direct knowledge; the last was Bhadrabāhu.

The Nandī's twofold division of scripture: what 'enters the limbs' (the twelve Aṅgas, composed by the gaṇadharas) and what is 'outside the limbs' (composed by later elders); the latter is further divided into kālika (read at set times) and utkālika (read at any time).

A 'recitation' — an assembly of monks to collect and fix the scripture: at Pāṭaliputra after the famine, at Mathurā under Skandila (and at Valabhī under Nāgārjuna), and at Valabhī under Devarddhigaṇi, where the canon was written down.

The oldest layer of commentary on the canon: Prakrit verses (gāthā) explaining key words by the method of nikṣepa and adding narratives; ten are ascribed to Bhadrabāhu. Followed by the bhāṣya (verse), cūrṇi (Prakrit-Sanskrit prose) and ṭīkā or vṛtti (Sanskrit) layers.
A prose commentary in mixed Prakrit and Sanskrit on a canonical text and its niryukti or bhāṣya (e.g. Jinadāsa's on the Niśītha and Āvaśyaka), rich in narrative.

The 'half-Māgadhī' Prakrit of the Śvetāmbara canon, held to be the language in which Mahāvīra taught; the Jina's speech in it is understood by gods, humans and animals each in their own tongue (an atiśaya).

A 'gift' or treatise-section: in the Pūrvas, a subdivision of a vastu (the Kaṣāyapāhuḍa is such a prābhṛta); in Kundakunda's usage, a treatise (Samayapāhuḍa, the eight Pāhuḍas). Tradition credits Kundakunda with eighty-four pāhuḍas.

The fifth and last ground of monastic judgment: the practice established by accepted teachers, used when no higher authority (supernormal knowledge, scripture, instruction, tradition) is available; the Jītakalpa fixes atonements by it.
In the fourfold nikṣepa, a word applied to a representation of the thing — an image, painting or token — whether it resembles it or not.
The canonical ground for venerating the Jina 'placed' in an image (sthāpanā-jina), and for the sthāpanācārya (a token of the teacher used in rites).

One of the fourteen 'ways of search' through which souls are investigated in the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama and Gommaṭasāra (destiny, sense, body, activity, sex, passion, knowledge, restraint, perception, leśyā, capacity for liberation, right faith, rationality, nourishment).
'Sky-clad': the naked monk, and the tradition that holds complete nudity necessary for the fully renounced and for liberation.
Called Boṭika (Boḍiya) in Śvetāmbara sources, which trace it to Śivabhūti's schism.
'White-clad': the tradition whose monks and nuns wear white garments, keeping clothes and bowls as instruments of restraint, not as possessions.
Called Śvetapaṭa in Digambara sources, which trace it to a famine-time relaxation of practice.

Name of the extinct order that combined naked monasticism with acceptance of women's liberation and the kevalin's eating; the name has been explained from 'yāpanīya' ('that which sustains / keeps going'), a word in the formula of monastic greeting (low confidence).
'Image-worshipper': the Śvetāmbaras who worship consecrated images of the Jinas in temples (also Derāvāsī, 'temple-dweller/goer', and Mandiramārgī).
'Dweller in halls': the aniconic Śvetāmbaras, whose mendicants stay in plain halls (sthānaka) rather than near temples, and who reject image worship.
The Śvetāmbara order founded by Ācārya Bhikṣu (1760); the name is explained as 'the path of thirteen' (after the first thirteen monks or laymen) or as 'your path, O Lord' (terā = 'yours').
Also the name of an unconnected 17th-c. Digambara reform (against the bhaṭṭārakas and fresh offerings), contrasted with the Bīsapantha.

A monastic lineage or order among the Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjakas (Tapā, Kharatara, Añcala and others), with its own succession of ācāryas, ritual details and calendar; earlier sources use gaṇa, kula and śākhā.
The fourfold community founded by each Tīrthaṅkara: monks (sādhu), nuns (sādhvī), laymen (śrāvaka) and laywomen (śrāvikā); itself called the 'ford' (tīrtha).

A clothed Digambara cleric heading a seat (maṭha), who administers temples, institutions and learning and conducts rites; authority of the Bīsapantha, rejected by the Digambara Terāpantha; seats at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa, Mūḍabidri, Kolhapur and elsewhere.

The practice of monks residing permanently in temples and managing their property, attacked by Haribhadra and by the Kharatara reformers, who insisted on vasativāsa, living in lodgings offered by laypeople.

A clothed resident Śvetāmbara religious of the late medieval period, less strict than a full mendicant, often keeping property and practising astrology or medicine; the reformers who founded the Sthānakavāsīs and revived Mūrtipūjaka mendicancy reacted against them.

A 'concealer' (schismatic) who, while accepting the Jina's teaching, denied one point of it and would not be corrected — seven in the Sthānāṅga (from Jamāli to Goṣṭhāmāhila), eight with the Boṭikas in the Āvaśyaka commentaries.
Śvetāmbara name for the Digambaras, as followers of Śivabhūti's schism of 609 years after the nirvāṇa.
The written code of the Terāpanth order laid down by Ācārya Bhikṣu (a single ācārya, no personal disciples, collective discipline), celebrated in the annual Maryādā Mahotsava (from Jayācārya's time).

A 'ford-maker': an omniscient Jina who, after attaining kevala, teaches the dharma and founds the fourfold community (the 'ford' across saṃsāra); twenty-four appear in each half of the time-cycle, by the ripening of the tīrthaṅkara-nāma-karma bound in an earlier life.
The Śvetāmbaras include a woman, Mallī, among the Tīrthaṅkaras of this era.
All Tīrthaṅkaras are male; the Tīrthaṅkara does not eat after omniscience.

cross_language.note: variant form used e.g. in Tattvārthasūtra 6.24

equivalents.note: the same word in its variant form; the Pāśupata use of 'tīrthakara' for their own teachers is a different referent

definitions.definition: Variant of tīrthaṅkara, the ford-making Jina (used in the Digambara Tattvārthasūtra 6.24).

A 'holder of the group': one of the chief disciples of a Tīrthaṅkara, who hears his teaching and composes it as scripture and leads a section of the community; Mahāvīra had eleven, headed by Indrabhūti Gautama.
A fully initiated Jain monk who has taken the five great vows for life; the fifth rank saluted in the Namaskāra ('all the sādhus in the world').
A fully initiated Jain nun with the five great vows; in Śvetāmbara orders nuns outnumber monks, are led by a pravartinī and follow rules such as never going unclothed.
The Digambara nun is called āryikā; she keeps one white sari and is not regarded as fully without possessions.

A Digambara nun: she wears a single white garment, lives with other nuns, eats seated (not in the hand like the monk), and in Digambara teaching cannot in this body pass beyond the fifth stage in the full sense because she keeps a garment.

The advanced Digambara lay renunciants of the eleventh pratimā: the kṣullaka keeps two cloths and a bowl, the ailaka a single loincloth and eats from the hand; the next step is muni-initiation into nudity. Women may become kṣullikās.
A Jain laywoman, fourth member of the fourfold community; the Kalpa Sūtra counts 318,000 in Mahāvīra's time, headed by Sulasā and Revatī.
An 'illustrious person' of the universal history: in each half-cycle sixty-three — 24 Tīrthaṅkaras, 12 cakravartins, 9 baladevas, 9 vāsudevas and 9 prativāsudevas.

One of the nine half-world-conquerors of each half-cycle, always paired with an elder brother baladeva and opposed by a prativāsudeva whom he kills; Lakṣmaṇa and Kṛṣṇa are the eighth and ninth. Because of the violence of their lives vāsudevas go to hell, though Kṛṣṇa will be a future Tīrthaṅkara.
One of the patriarchs who, at the end of the age of wish-fulfilling trees, guided people and instituted the first laws; the last was Nābhi, father of Ṛṣabha (lists of seven or fourteen).
A Tīrthaṅkara now teaching in the Mahāvideha regions, where the fourth age always prevails; twenty are counted, the first being Sīmandhara.
'Knotless' — free of the knots of possessions and passions; the old name of Jain mendicants (Pali 'nigaṇṭha') and of Mahāvīra as Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta; Digambaras take it as requiring nudity.

cross_language.note: as used in the Pali canon of Jain monks

definitions.definition: Tamil name for Jain monks (from śramaṇa), common in Tamil literature and in the hymns of the Nāyaṉmārs who opposed them.
Tamil form of Arhat, the Jina, invoked in the opening verses of Tamil Jain works.
Virtue, dharma: in the Jain didactic works (Nālaṭiyār) the right conduct to be done now, before wealth, youth and the body pass away.
Renunciation: in the Nālaṭiyār the wise one's giving up of attachment on seeing the body's impurity and the world's transience.

One of the five 'auspicious events' in every Tīrthaṅkara's life — descent into the womb (cyavana/garbha), birth (janma), renunciation (dīkṣā), omniscience (kevala-jñāna) and final liberation (nirvāṇa) — celebrated by the gods and re-enacted in temple consecrations and festivals.

The 'divine sound' of the omniscient Jina: a single, undifferentiated sound issuing from his whole body at set times, without movement of lips, which the gaṇadharas render into scripture and all beings understand.
Śvetāmbaras speak rather of the Jina's speech in Ardhamāgadhī, understood by all beings in their own languages.
One of the thirty-four 'excellences' (supernatural features) of a Tīrthaṅkara — some from birth, some arising with omniscience, some produced by the gods.

One of the eight 'marvels' attending the omniscient Jina, shown in his images: the aśoka tree, the rain of flowers, the divine sound, the fly-whisks, the lion-throne, the halo, the divine drum and the triple parasol.
The emblem by which each Tīrthaṅkara's otherwise identical image is recognized, carved on the pedestal: the bull of Ṛṣabha, the conch of Nemi, the serpent of Pārśva, the lion of Mahāvīra, and so on.
The removal of Mahāvīra's embryo by Hariṇaigameṣin, at Śakra's command, from the brāhmaṇī Devānandā to the kṣatriyāṇī Triśalā; counted among the ten 'wonders' of this era.
Rejected: Mahāvīra was conceived by Triśalā alone.

One of the ten extraordinary events of this descending half-cycle that ordinarily should not happen (a woman Tīrthaṅkara, the embryo transfer, an attack on a Jina, a fruitless first sermon, and others).
The divine cloth placed by Śakra on Mahāvīra's shoulder at his renunciation, which he kept for about thirteen months before going naked.

A secret resolve limiting the conditions under which a mendicant will accept alms — like Mahāvīra's vow, fulfilled by the shackled Candanā, to accept food only from a captive princess with shaven head, one foot inside the threshold, weeping.
An affliction inflicted by gods, humans or animals on a meditating ascetic, to be borne with equanimity; Mahāvīra's twelve years were full of them, and Pārśva's attacker was Kamaṭha.
Recollection of former births, a form of sensory-mental knowledge that often awakens renunciation — as when Mahāvīra reminded Megha of his elephant birth.
Nakedness, the first of the Digambara monk's special root qualities; required for full renunciation and liberation.
Either nakedness (the Jinakalpa mode, followed by Mahāvīra and early ascetics) or wearing few, poor garments; one of the twenty-two hardships; not required now.
Naked monasticism kept as the rule, with clothing allowed by exception (apavāda-liṅga) and for women.

The 'mode of the Jinas': the solitary, naked (or nearly equipment-less), hand-eating ascetic life of highest rigour, open in the Śvetāmbara view only to those with special capacities and discontinued after Jambū.
The 'mode of the elders': mendicant life in a community with the minimum of permitted clothing, bowls and equipment — the valid mode for the present age.
The cloth covering the mouth, worn constantly by Sthānakavāsī and Terāpanthī mendicants to avoid harming beings of the air by breath and speech.
Mūrtipūjaka mendicants carry it in the hand and hold it before the mouth when speaking; laity use it in rites.
The woollen whisk ('dust-remover', ogho) with which Śvetāmbara mendicants gently sweep insects from their path and seat; the chief sign of initiation.
The whisk of naturally shed peacock feathers carried by Digambara monks and nuns to remove small beings without harm; with the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) and a scripture it is all they own.
'Hand as bowl': the Digambara monk eats once a day, standing, from his cupped hands, at a house where he is properly received.
Plucking out the hair of head and face by hand, at initiation and periodically thereafter, as a practice of endurance and non-attachment to the body.
The mendicant's alms-round, 'grazing like a cow' or taking 'like a bee' a little from many houses, accepting only food not prepared for him and free of the faults of alms.
The bee's way of alms: taking a little from each house as the bee from flowers, harming none (Daśavaikālika 1).

The four months of the rains during which mendicants stop wandering and stay in one place to avoid harming the many beings that appear, the season of teaching, austerities and Paryuṣaṇa for the laity.

equivalents.note: the Buddhist rains retreat serves the same purpose of not wandering in the rains

definitions.definition: Not eating at night, added as a sixth vow for mendicants and a basic rule for laity, since small beings cannot be seen in the dark.
The 'fourfold restraint' taught by Pārśva — from violence, falsehood, theft and possessions — which Mahāvīra expanded into five great vows by making chastity explicit.

cross_language.note: the Pali canon attributes a 'fourfold restraint' to Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta

definitions.definition: The rules of correct monastic conduct and daily routine (the ten points of Uttarādhyayana 26; the rainy-season rules of the Kalpa Sūtra).

The 'great initiation' (baḍī dīkṣā): the second, definitive ordination in which the novice is placed in the vows one by one after learning the Daśavaikālika's fourth chapter; also the name of the second of the five kinds of conduct.
The eight-day festival at the height of the rains (Bhādrapada), of fasting, confession and forgiveness, with the public reading of the Kalpa Sūtra, ending in Saṃvatsarī.
The Digambaras keep the ten days of Das Lakṣaṇa (the ten dharmas) at the same season.

The last day of Paryuṣaṇa, the day of the annual confession (saṃvatsarī pratikramaṇa) and of asking forgiveness of all beings; kept on the fourth or fifth of bright Bhādrapada depending on the tradition (Kālaka's change).
'May my wrongdoing be fruitless' — the formula of repentance in confession, and the greeting by which Jains ask one another's forgiveness at Saṃvatsarī.

literal: may my misdeed be in vain

definitions.definition: Asking and granting forgiveness — to all beings in daily and annual confession, and person to person at Paryuṣaṇa; the Kalpa Sūtra makes it the condition of being a true 'fulfiller' of the discipline.

equivalents.note: the Buddhist end-of-rains 'invitation' to be admonished is a comparable communal reconciliation; the contents differ

definitions.definition: Forbearance, the first of the ten dharmas ('supreme forbearance', uttama-kṣamā), the virtue by which anger is conquered.

The ten-day Digambara festival of the rains devoted in turn to the ten dharmas (forbearance, humility, straightforwardness, purity, truth, restraint, austerity, renunciation, non-possession, chastity), ending with forgiveness.
Taking the four refuges — the Arhats, the Siddhas, the Sādhus and the dharma taught by the omniscient — recited with the 'four auspicious things' and 'four highest things'.
A consecrated image of a Jina (always in meditation, seated or standing), a support for recalling his qualities; worshipped with material (dravya) and inner (bhāva) worship.
Not to be worshipped: the canon gives no such injunction and worship harms beings.
A shrine or image of the Jina (the Mūrtipūjaka reading of 'ceiya' in the canon).
The Sthānakavāsīs read canonical 'ceiya' in many places as knowledge, a sage or a sacred tree rather than an image-shrine (a disputed reading).

Material worship with substances (water, sandal, flowers, incense, lamp, rice, sweets, fruit — the eightfold pūjā), proper to householders, and inner worship by praise and meditation, proper to all; the first is a means to the second.
The 'great head-anointing' of the colossal image of Bāhubali at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa, held about every twelve years, pouring water, milk, sugarcane juice, saffron and other substances.
Liberation of women in a female body — affirmed: the canon speaks of women siddhas and a woman Tīrthaṅkara.
Affirmed and argued: the three jewels are not deficient in women.
Denied: a woman cannot give up clothing and lacks the bodily constitution for the highest meditation; she may be reborn as a man and then be liberated.
The omniscient takes morsel-food (kavalāhāra) while his body lasts; hunger, thirst and the other feeling-karma hardships occur in him.
Affirmed and argued by Śākaṭāyana.
Denied: the omniscient is free of hunger and thirst (two of the eighteen faults) and his body is sustained without morsel-food.

Physical sex (the bodily marks) as against psychological sex (the rise of the sexual-desire karma); Digambaras say liberation occurs from any bhāva-veda but only from the male dravya-veda, and read canonical 'female siddhas' as referring to bhāva-veda.
Compassion, one of the marks of right faith; the elephant's compassion for the hare won Megha human birth.
Distinguished into worldly (laukika) compassion that preserves bodily life and spiritual (lokottara) compassion that leads beings to restraint; only the second is dharma.
'Supramundane' dharma — acts that stop karmic inflow and foster self-restraint — as against laukika (worldly, social) duty, which may be good conduct but is not spiritual dharma.
Compassion for living beings, which must be guided by knowledge ('first knowledge, then compassion').
'Own-doctrine / own-self': the soul abiding in its own faith, knowledge and conduct, as against para-samaya, the soul identified with karmic matter (Samayasāra 2).

In Kundakunda, the self (as 'that which knows and moves in its own nature') and the doctrine about it — hence Samayasāra, 'the essence of the self'; elsewhere in Jain usage also the smallest unit of time and equanimity (samatā).

The standpoint of ultimate reality, which describes the self as it is in itself — pure, undivided, unbound; called 'real' (bhūtārtha) by Kundakunda. Right faith relies on it, while the conventional standpoint is needed to teach.

equivalents.note: both name the ultimate level from which the conventional description is transcended; Kundakunda's niścaya describes an individual pure soul, not a single Brahman

definitions.definition: The conventional standpoint, which describes the soul through distinctions and relations (as having knowledge, faith, conduct, bondage, stages); 'unreal' (abhūtārtha) but indispensable for teaching, like speaking to a foreigner in his own tongue.

equivalents.note: both name the conventional level used to teach; the Jain standpoint does not declare the world an illusion

definitions.definition: Pure cognitive activity, the soul's abiding in itself beyond both good (śubha) and bad (aśubha) activity; good activity (devotion, vows) brings merit but still binds, pure activity alone liberates.

Instrumental and substantial cause: in Kundakunda's analysis the soul's impure states and karmic matter are occasions (nimitta) for each other, but each is the substantial cause (upādāna) only of its own modifications.
Attachment and aversion, the 'seeds of karma' (Uttarādhyayana 32.7); in the Kaṣāyapāhuḍa, pejja and dosa, under which the four passions are classed.
The reliable authority: the Jina, free of the eighteen faults (including hunger and thirst), omniscient, and teacher of the good; right faith is faith in the āpta, the scripture and the teacher.
Knowledge, of five kinds (mati, śruta, avadhi, manaḥparyaya, kevala), the soul's own nature; to be gained before compassion can be rightly exercised.
Vigilance, never being careless for a moment ('samayaṃ goyama mā pamāyae'); the seventh guṇasthāna is named 'apramatta-saṃyata'.
'Accomplishment': the perfecting of right faith, knowledge, conduct and austerity, especially as brought to completion at the end of life under a guide.
One who has reconciled with all at Paryuṣaṇa is an 'ārādhaka' (fulfiller) of the discipline.
Human effort, affirmed by Mahāvīra against Gośāla's fatalism in the argument of the potter's pots.

The six 'spokes' (ara) of each half of the time-wheel, from 'very happy' (suṣamā-suṣamā) to 'very unhappy' (duḥṣamā-duḥṣamā); Tīrthaṅkaras appear only in the third and fourth; the present is the fifth (duḥṣamā), in which liberation from this region is no longer possible.
